<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
{\rm  A {\it groupoid} ${\mathcal Z} \rightrightarrows {\mathcal B}$ consists of two sets, $\mathcal Z$ and $\mathcal B$, called, respectively, the set of {\it arrows} and the set of {\it objects}, related by two surjective {\it projection maps}, $\alpha, \beta: {\mathcal Z} \to {\mathcal B}$, called the {\it source} map and the {\it target} map, respectively. Just as in the case of a group, an associative operation (the {\it product} or {\it composition} of arrows) is defined in $\mathcal Z$. This operation, however, can only be carried out between two arrows $u, v \in {\mathcal Z}$ if the ``tip-to-tail'' condition
\begin{equation}
\beta(u)=\alpha(v)
\end{equation}
is satisfied. The result, denoted by $vu$, satisfies the conditions
\begin{equation}
\alpha(vu)=\alpha(u),\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\; \beta(vu)=\beta(v).
\end{equation}
For each object $b \in {\mathcal B}$ a unique {\it identity arrow} $\epsilon(b)$ exists such that $\epsilon(u)\,u=u$, for every $u \in {\mathcal Z}$ such that $\beta(u)=b$, and $ u\,\epsilon(u)=u$, for every  $u \in {\mathcal Z}$ such that $\alpha(u)=u$. For each arrow $u \in {\mathcal Z}$ there is a (unique) {\it inverse arrow} $u^{-1} \in {\mathcal Z}$ such that $u^{-1}\,u=\epsilon(\alpha(u))$, and $u\,u^{-1}=\epsilon(\beta(u))$.
}
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- rem-1: body_md -->
{\rm In spite of its length, the definition of a groupoid is a rather intuitive rendering of the main features of examples such as the set of material isomorphisms of a body, or the set of operations that preserve the appearance of a tiled floor (including the mutual exchange of congruent tiles). A groupoid can also be regarded as a generalization of the concept of equivalence relation, a generalization that takes into account that an object may be equivalent to another (including itself) in a multiplicity of ways.
}
<!-- end rem-1 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
{\rm A groupoid is {\it transitive} if there is at least one arrow between every pair of objects}
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- example-1: body_md -->
{\rm A body all of whose points are made of the same material is said to be {\it uniform}. Consequently, a body is uniform if, and only if, its material groupoid is transitive.}
<!-- end example-1 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
{\rm An elastic body $\mathcal B$ is a {\it weighted n-ary elastic composite} (or simply a {\it composite}) if the following conditions are satisfied:
\begin{enumerate}
\item The constitutive equation can be expressed as a sum
\begin{equation}
{\bf T}=\sum_{\alpha=1}^n  k_\alpha(X)\;{\bf f}_\alpha ({\bf F}, X),
\end{equation}
where each of the coefficient scalar functions $k_\alpha$ is positive definite and
\begin{equation}
\sum_{\alpha=1}^n k_\alpha = 1.
\end{equation}
\item Each of the functions ${\bf f}_\alpha \;(\alpha=1,...,n)$ satisfies the {\it uniformity} property
\begin{equation}
 {\bf f}_\alpha({\bf F}, X_2) = {\bf f}_\alpha({\bf F\, P}^\alpha_{12}, X_1),\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\forall \; {\bf F} \in GL(3,{\mathbb R}),
\end{equation}
for each pair points $X_1, X_2 \in {\mathcal B}$, where ${\bf P}^\alpha_{12}$ is a material isomorphism between $X_1$ and $X_2$ associated with the function ${\bf f}_\alpha$.
\end{enumerate}
}
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- definition-4: body_md -->
\label{def:weightedunif} {\rm A composite $\mathcal B$ is said to enjoy the property of {\it weighted uniformity} if for every pair of points $X_1, X_2 \in {\mathcal B}$, the intersection of the sets of material isomorphisms between these points of all the constituents is non-empty, namely
\begin{equation}
\bigcap\limits_{\alpha=1}^n {\mathcal P}^\alpha_{12}  \ne \emptyset,
\end{equation}
where ${\mathcal P}^\alpha_{12}$ denotes the collection of all material isomorphisms ${\bf P}^\alpha_{12}$ between $X_1$ and $X_2$ in the constituent $\alpha$.
}
<!-- end definition-4 -->
<!-- rem-2: body_md -->
{\rm If each of the volume fractions $k_\alpha$ is spatially constant, weighted uniformity implies uniformity, as defined in \cite{jmps}).
}
<!-- end rem-2 -->
<!-- definition-5: body_md -->
{\rm A {\it double groupoid} is a set ${\mathcal Q}$ equipped with 2 groupoid structures
whose bases are themselves ordinary groupoids ${\mathcal H}$ and ${\mathcal V}$, with a common base $\mathcal B$. Denoting the compositions of the first and second groupoid structures of $\mathcal Q$ by $\odot_V$ and $\odot_H$, respectively,
the following {\it compatibility condition} must be satisfied
\begin{equation} \label{dg5again}
({\mathbb A}\odot_H{\mathbb B})\odot_V({\mathbb C}\odot_H{\mathbb D})=({\mathbb A}\odot_V{\mathbb C})\odot_H({\mathbb B}\odot_V{\mathbb D})\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\forall\,{\mathbb A},{\mathbb B},{\mathbb C},{\mathbb D} \in {\mathcal Q}
\end{equation}
whenever the operations are possible. Other conditions of compatibility between the two structures can be summarized by stating that the structure maps of each groupoid structure of $\mathcal Q$ are groupoid morphisms with respect to the other structure.\footnote{These properties will be described below more explicitly. A groupoid morphism is a map (or {\it functor}) that assigns to each arrow of one groupoid an arrow of the other groupoid, and that preserves identities and compositions.}

}
<!-- end definition-5 -->
<!-- rem-3: body_md -->
{\rm The {\it double source map} assigning to each square $\mathbb A$ its sources in the horizontal and vertical structures, ${\tilde \alpha}_H({\mathbb A}), {\tilde \alpha}_V({\mathbb A})$, is often assumed to be surjective. The graphical representation of this assumption is that a right angle made of a horizontal and a vertical arrow issuing from a common corner in $\mathcal B$ can always be completed (not necessarily uniquely) to a square in $\mathcal Q$. This is known as the {\it filling condition}.
}
<!-- end rem-3 -->
<!-- example-2: body_md -->
{\rm A useful example of a double groupoid is the {\it coarse double groupoid} $\square({\mathcal H},{\mathcal V})$, generated by two groupoids, $\mathcal H$ and $\mathcal V$, with a common base set. It consists of all the possible squares that can be formed using the two groupoids as sides. Any double groupoid can be naturally mapped as an inclusion into the coarse double groupoid generated by its side groupoids.
}
<!-- end example-2 -->
<!-- definition-6: body_md -->
\label{def:core} {\rm 
The {\it core} ${\mathcal C}_{\mathcal Q}$ of a double groupoid $\mathcal Q$ is an ordinary groupoid consisting of the collection of all squares $\mathbb A$ for which the two source arrows $s$ and $\hat s$ are, respectively, the units of $\mathcal H$ and $\mathcal V$ at the point $X=\alpha_H\left(\hat{\alpha}_V({\mathbb A})\right)=\alpha_V\left(\hat{\alpha}_H({\mathbb A})\right)$.
}
<!-- end definition-6 -->
<!-- prop-1: body_md -->
{\rm A binary composite satisfies the condition of weighted uniformity if, and only if, the core of its material double groupoid is transitive.
}
<!-- end prop-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Since every square of $\mathcal Q$ is commutative, it follows from Definition \ref{def:core} that every pair $(t, {\hat t}) \in {\mathcal C}_{\mathcal Q}$ satisfies the condition $t={\hat t}$. The proposition is an immediate consequence of Definition \ref{def:weightedunif}
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- rem-4: body_md -->
{\rm This construction is most probably equivalent to the Cartesian product of the groiupoid ${\mathcal G}\rightrightarrows{\mathcal B}$ times the pair groupoid ${\bf C}\times {\bf C} \rightrightarrows {\bf C}$.
}
<!-- end rem-4 -->
